"We are putting in serious consideration on the sense of tempo."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"This time we are putting in serious consideration on the sense of tempo, back at Dawntrail we were being really careful in depicting new lands, new cultures, new encounters and this greatly slowed down the pacing on story progression. The fact that this did not align with the player's motivation of 'keep moving forward' shows shortcomings on my part as the director.

"For Evercold, segments that focus on above-mentioned elements are moved to side quests, and we made it so that players can enjoy them at their own pace after, and pay our attention to the sense of tempo," via the r/FFXIV subreddit.

As PC Gamer's premier 'I think too much about the story Dawntrail could've been' person (which is a proper, official title, don't look it up), I have some thoughts about this.

Now to be clear, this is a translated quote from a group interview, and while Yoshi-P is certainly involved in the process of writing any expansion, he's a game director, so he's got an overarching view rather than a handle on the nitty-gritty of a given storyline. However, I don't think the issue in Dawntrail was its over-emphasis on worldbuilding, it was a lack of interest in how that worldbuilding connected to character.

Sure, the whole 'talk to three people' questlines get deservedly dunked on as a clumsy vehicle for how this stuff gets conveyed, but I don't really have any problem with how Dawntrail sets up the continent of Tural itself. As a matter of fact, I think the baseline is all very interesting—a fledgling nation under a first king at the end of his life, forced to reckon with how succession will work? That's a fun setup.

The stumbling of Dawntrail is in how none of these worldbuilding details had knock-on effects for the characters in any real, meaningful way. We learn about these cultures, and they either barely come up again or they add little to the core emotional conflicts that the characters are going through, with the exception of the Mamool Ja and the Skydeep Cenote.

Gulool Ja Ja, the warrior-king soon to abdicate the throne, basically does no wrong throughout all the stories we learn of him (aside from his raising of Zoraal Ja, which isn't really explored anyway) giving absolutely nothing for the main cast to reflect on. Wuk Lamat's relationship with her siblings is never meaningfully or memorably explored in the context of the societies she's learning about.

Even the rite of succession messes up clean opportunities—there's a whole segment where contestants are randomly assigned to partners, and rather than use this as an opportunity to have Wuk Lamat, say, paired with someone she doesn't like, she just gets put with Koana and nothing really happens as a result.

Textured worldbuilding isn't the issue—the issue is that worldbuilding should generally feed back into the overarching themes and narrative. I'm not sure simply offloading all of it into the story's sidequests is the answer, rather than having a considered effort to make it interesting and relevant to the characters at hand.

But again, I'm not expecting Yoshi-P to sate my hunger for nitty-gritty nuance through the filter of translation in a group interview—and the current Evercold introductory patch story does give me hope, given there's already been some effective show-not-tell worldbuilding in it. The fact Visna freaks out about us approaching without stating our brand is great, it immediately sets the stakes for life in this ice-covered world without beating us over the head with it. So there is genuine hope that FF14's story really is returning to form.

#3834. Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic's next DLC is set to expand the city building sim into the one place not corrupted by capitalism: SPACE

Following not the inherent liberal capitalistic framework of city builders like SimCity but instead a revolutionary (sorry) interpretation of planning and logistical simulation that prioritises centralisation and minute detail, Hooded Horse and 3DIVISION's Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic offers a tense, socialist look at what a citybuilder could be. Fellow contributor Sin Vega, in her 1.0 review, described it like this: "You have to build things to demolish things. That might be Workers & Resources in a nutshell. You're not managing budgets (money is exclusively for imports/exports), you're organising stuff." Now, having previously expanding out of the Soviet Republic and across the globe with the World Maps DLC, the next step for socialist citybuilding is, of course, space. Our Edwin outright predicted this two years ago, correctly calling that "the logical endgame here is to go to space." Good on him.

The Space Program DLC, set to release on November 23rd, will add a variety of new technologies and types of industry to the builder. It looks like it'll focus on not only the actual rockets that get into space, and the spectacle of it all, but also the huge amounts of science and industry that get to the point of rockets not exploding upon takeoff. For example, while it's all well and good for Space Program's scientists to be able to design rockets that are capable of remaining together for long enough to land safely, the designs they dream of still have to be built, meaning that industrial pipelines must be effectively centralised to ensure that every single component is of high quality and arriving in the required quantity.

The update also specifies the Sputnik and Vostok programs as elements of the expansion, implying a close historical aspect to it — though, elsewhere, "an unprecedented duel with nature" is mentioned, which is referring to either the simple harshness of space or aliens. Jury's out. A 1960s campaign will be a star feature of the DLC, which is described as a place for players to learn the new mechanics "in relative peace, surrounded by a happy, healthy, and economically stable utopia." What an idea.

GTA 6 pre-loading opens November 10 for some

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is a 212GB download to pre-load, Rockstar has confirmed, and that pre-load will be available two days early for digital buyers.

In a new post, Rockstar notes that "the pre-load file" for GTA 6 "will require up to 212 GB depending on your device, so make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible." PS5 and Xbox Series X file sizes may differ slightly; it was previously claimed that GTA 6 GB size was 210 on PS5. Pre-load downloads and final install sizes can also differ noticeably.

If you've pre-ordered GTA 6, you may have noticed an order form noting that pre-loading opens on November 12. Rockstar has now clarified that "digital pre-loading on PlayStation 5 will begin on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time in your respective time zone."

On Xbox Series X, "pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT."

And, per previous communications, "code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12."

Rockstar has a whole pre-load FAQ for those unfamiliar with the process or simply looking to read something, anything about GTA 6 during this final wait. If that's you, witness Jasmine's bold take: GTA 6 sounds like an RPG – so why deny it?

Rockstar also rolled out one final bonus purchase for GTA 6: a double-sided poster of the game's cover art and map, available for $1 separately or for free with another purchase on Rockstar's own merch store.
